notes: The standard opening position, played as England.

order_set_labels.label: reasonable
order_set_labels.reason: - Moving the fleet from Edinburgh to the Norwegian Sea makes sense because it can then threaten Norway. - Moving the fleet from London to the North Sea makes sense because it can then threaten Holland, Denmark, and Norway. - Moving the army from Liverpool to Yorkshire makes sense because it can then convoy over the fleet in the North Sea, and it can also protect London if France moves into the English Channel.

order_set_labels.label: reasonable
order_set_labels.reason: Moving Fleet Edinburgh to the North Sea makes sense. There is no unit that can stop it from getting into the North Sea. From the North Sea, the fleet threatens Norway, Denmark, and Holland. Moving Liverpool to Yorkshire makes sense. The army is now able to convoy across the North Sea. The fleet from London to the English Channel makes sense. It prevents France from getting into the English Channel, which threatens London. It also puts the fleet in a position to threaten Belgium or Brest.

order_set_labels.label: reasonable
order_set_labels.reason: This is not an especially strong order set, but it is not totally unreasonable. The two fleet movements make sense. The army moving to Wales is a little bit questionable. From Wales, the army can only convoy over the English Channel. Capturing the English Channel is less than guaranteed. If France bounces the fleet out of the English Channel, the army in Wales is at a dead end.

order_set_labels.label: unreasonable
order_set_labels.reason: The fleet in Edinburgh and the fleet in London both move to the North Sea and are guaranteed to bounce back to their original positions. There is no strategic reason to do a self-bounce here because none of the positions in question are directly threatened by any other nation.

order_set_labels.label: reasonable
order_set_labels.reason: This is a weak order set because moving the army to Wales is a dead end. The only advantage of having the army in Wales is that it can protect London if France decides to move to the English Channel, but the same is true if the army moves to Yorkshire. If the army moves to Yorkshire, it can protect London and can also be convoyed across the fleet in the North Sea.
